title: Why You Should Never Ask Students To Apologize
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that teachers should never ask or require students to apologize for misbehavior, even though the instinct feels right. An apology prompted by an authority figure carries no meaning and is itself proof that the apology was not real. Pressuring a student also short-circuits the natural process of reflection, so guilt never has a chance to weigh on the conscience, and it forces the wronged child to sit through a charade. Linsin holds that real accountability comes from a predetermined consequence applied consistently, not from a staged apology. When students understand the boundaries that protect everyone's right to learn, empathy and a voluntary apology tend to follow over time. His conclusion is that a consistently followed classroom management plan, delivered amid kindness and clear leadership, is what produces genuine apologies.
points: An apology that a person in authority prompts is meaningless to the receiver and demonstrates that the apology was not sincere.
Requiring an apology undermines reflection because the student complies to get the teacher off their back instead of feeling the weight of their own guilt.
Forced apologies humiliate the wronged student and let the teacher feel they handled the incident well when they did not.
Accountability comes from a predetermined, consistently applied consequence, which is what most effectively produces a contrite heart.
A genuine apology is a by-product of a consistently followed classroom management plan, and behavior can improve even when no apology is offered.
quotes: When you know the apology you’ve received was prompted by a person in authority, it means nothing. It’s proof, even, that the apology wasn’t real.
The indignity of having to listen to your tormentor’s forced apology is one reason why restorative justice practices not only don’t work, but often cause deep resentment.
If the apology doesn’t originate from within the misbehaving student, then it isn’t sincere. It’s a hoop to jump through to get the teacher off their back.
The wronged party knows this. It’s all a charade meant only to satisfy the teacher, who can then carry on self-satisfied and convinced they handled it well.
Accountability in the classroom can only come from a predetermined consequence. It’s the certainty of breaking a rule that harmed another that most effectively causes a contrite heart.

Understanding how their actions affect others often triggers a desire to make amends. Done right, and over time, accountability causes the kind of self-reflection and empathy that triggers an apology.
It’s prompted by a consistently followed classroom management plan.
